# Questions & Hypotheses

1.	 How do adult birds with active nests change their provisioning behavior during hot periods? We hypothesized that adult birds will
a.	 (H1) reduce their provisioning rates during hot periods because they must put more time and/or energy into thermoregulation to avoid hyperthermia
b. (H1A) increase their provisioning rates during hot periods because they must deliver more energy to compensate for thermoregulatory costs to chicks (water or energy)

2. What mediates how responsive provisioning rates are to temperature?
a. (H1) Less optimal foraging conditions over the prior day will make provisioning rates less responsive to temperature because adults will respond to their chicks being hungrier when they were fed less over the prior day.
b. (H2) females in better condition (mass/tarsus) would be less likely than females in worse condition to reduce their visits during hot periods because they are able to mobilize the energy required to engage in more energetically costly active thermoregulatory behaviors and 
c.	(H3) Females with higher baseline cort will be less responsive to temperature - possibly because they are exposing themselves to suboptimal conditions
d. (H4) Females with higher stress-induced cort will be more responsive to temperature because they have been experiencing their environment as stressful, and therefore may not have extra energy to put towards thermoregulation during hot periods.

3.	How does heat affect female body condition and stress status? baseline and stress-induced?
a.	H1: Females that experienced worse heat over the prior week will be more likely to show reduced body condition.
b. H2: females that experienced heat over the prior day will be more likely to show elevated baseline corticosterone levels because they may upregulate their HPA axis in response to more challenging heat conditions
c.	H3: females that experienced heat over the prior week will be more likely to show elevated stress-induced corticosterone levels because challenging environmental conditions are correlated with elevated stress-induced corticosterone levels.

4.	 Does body condition mediate cort response?
a.	(H1) females in better body condition would be more likely to show elevated baseline cort after a hot period because they have the energetic capacity to respond to stress
b.	(H2) Females in better body condition would be less likely to show elevated stress-induced corticosterone after a hot period than females in worse body condition.

Q4 no longer really fits with this new organization.

```{r setup,include = FALSE}
c <- read_rds("../data/cort_manytempmeasures.rds")

filter(c,blood_num %in% c("B486","B582","B584","B088","B107","B409","B338","B342","B129","B233","B302","B571","B546","B579","B580","B581","B583","B036","B087","B088","B517","B107","B412","B463","B329","B384","B130","B202","B301","B308","B273","B516","B581","B228")) %>% pull(Age)

## Calculate PC1 for female length measures, regress on mass, take residuals as condition value. Will need to go back to morphometrics I think. Match on attempt_id

g <- read_csv("../data/banding-and-morphometrics_proofed.csv") %>%
  filter(Age %in% c("SY","ASY","AHY"), Sex == "F") %>%
  dplyr::select(c(Nestbox,Species,band_number,`Banding Date`,`Fat Score`,`Right Wing Chord (mm)`,`Weight (g)`,`Tail Length (mm)`,`Skull Length (mm)`,`Nares-Tip (mm)`,`Tarsus (mm)`)) %>%
  mutate(across(`Right Wing Chord (mm)`:`Tarsus (mm)`,as.numeric)) %>%
  dplyr::filter(if_all(c(Species,`Right Wing Chord (mm)`,`Weight (g)`,`Tail Length (mm)`,`Skull Length (mm)`,`Nares-Tip (mm)`,`Tarsus (mm)`), ~ !is.na(.))) %>%
  mutate(pc1 = princomp(bind_cols(`Right Wing Chord (mm)`,`Tail Length (mm)`,`Skull Length (mm)`,`Nares-Tip (mm)`,`Tarsus (mm)`),na.action = na.exclude,fix_sign = TRUE)$scores[,1],
         res = lm(`Weight (g)` ~ pc1) %>% residuals(),
         .by = Species) %>%
  mutate(date = `Banding Date` %>% mdy() %>% force_tz("America/Los_Angeles"),
         year = year(date),
         julian_date = yday(date))
  
pc_webl <- princomp(bind_cols(dplyr::select(filter(g,Species == "WEBL"),c(`Right Wing Chord (mm)`,`Tail Length (mm)`,`Skull Length (mm)`,`Nares-Tip (mm)`,`Tarsus (mm)`))),na.action = na.exclude,fix_sign = TRUE)

summary(pc_webl)

fviz_pca_var(pc_webl, col.var = "black")

pc_tres <- princomp(bind_cols(dplyr::select(filter(g,Species == "TRES"),c(`Right Wing Chord (mm)`,`Tail Length (mm)`,`Skull Length (mm)`,`Nares-Tip (mm)`,`Tarsus (mm)`))),na.action = na.exclude,fix_sign = TRUE)

summary(pc_tres)

fviz_pca_var(pc_tres, col.var = "black")

names(g)

## Add condition measure (res) to p and c

p <- p %>%
  left_join(g %>% dplyr::select(c(Nestbox,band_number,Species,`Fat Score`,julian_date,year,res)),
             by = join_by(nestbox == Nestbox,species == Species,year == year)) %>% 
  mutate(date_diff = abs(julian_date.x - julian_date.y)) %>%          # or difftime() for POSIXct
  # filter(date_diff <= 20) %>%                    # threshold filter
  group_by(nestbox, species, start) %>%                       # one row from df1 per group
  arrange(date_diff, .by_group = TRUE) %>%              # smallest diff first
  slice(1) %>%                                          # tie → first row
  ungroup() %>%
  dplyr::select(!julian_date.y) %>%
  rename(julian_date = julian_date.x)

c <- c %>%
  mutate(year = as.numeric(as.character(year))) %>% 
  left_join(g %>% dplyr::select(c(Nestbox,Species,band_number,`Fat Score`,date,year,res)),
             by = join_by(Nestbox == Nestbox,Species == Species,year == year)) %>% 
  mutate(date_diff = difftime(sample_date, date)) %>%          # or difftime() for POSIXct
  # filter(date_diff <= 20) %>%                    # threshold filter
  group_by(Nestbox,Species,sample_date) %>%                       # one row from df1 per group
  arrange(date_diff, .by_group = TRUE) %>%              # smallest diff first
  slice(1) %>%                                          # tie → first row
  ungroup()

```

# Question 1: How do adult birds with active nests change their provisioning behavior during hot periods?

## Hypothesis 1: We hypothesized that adults will reduce their provisioning rates during hot periods because they must put more time and/or energy into thermoregulation to avoid hyperthermia

Prediction: provis peaks at intermediate temp

## (H1A) increase their provisioning rates during hot periods because they must deliver more energy to compensate for thermoregulatory costs to chicks (water or energy)

### WEBL

```{r}
           family = nbinom2(),
           ziformula = ~ (1|site:attempt_id),
           data = dplyr::filter(p,!is.na(mean_temp),

(tab <- comp %>%
  as.tibble() %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric),~round(.x,digits = 4)),
         P = `Pr(>Chisq)`) %>%
  dplyr::select(Model,AIC,Chisq,P) %>%
  mutate(across(c(AIC,Chisq), ~ round(.x, digits = 2)),
         P = if_else(P < 0.001,"<0.001",as.character(P))) %>% gt())

ss_year_webl_provis <- m_webl_q1h1$frame %>%
  group_by(year_fct) %>%
  summarize(count_ind = n(),count_attempt = n_distinct(attempt_id)) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(count = tibble(count_ind,count_attempt)) %>%
  dplyr::select(-c(count_ind, count_attempt)) %>%
  pivot_wider(values_from = count,names_from = year_fct) %>%
  as.tibble() %>% # rename(Habitat = 'habitat') %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(`2021` = replace_na(`2021`,list(count_ind = 0,count_attempt = 0))) %>%
  mutate(Total = `2021` + `2022` + `2023`) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(`2021` = paste0(`2021`$count_ind,", ",`2021`$count_attempt),
         `2022` = paste0(`2022`$count_ind,", ",`2022`$count_attempt),
         `2023` = paste0(`2023`$count_ind,", ",`2023`$count_attempt),
         Total = paste0(Total$count_ind,", ",Total$count_attempt)
  )

(t_ss_year_webl_provis <- ss_year_webl_provis %>% gt() %>%
    grand_summary_rows(fns = list(id = "Total") ~ {
      t <- str_split(.,", ",simplify = TRUE)
      t[,1] %>% as.numeric() %>% sum(na.rm = TRUE) %>% paste(t[,2] %>% as.numeric() %>% sum(na.rm = TRUE),sep = ", ")
    })
)
```

So provisining decreases with temp in forest, increases with temp in orchard, and does not change in grassland or row crop. Overall, no changes. So land cover is mediating responses to temp. So this means that the land cover interaction model is the one I should be using for provisioning. The causal links are interesting though - if condition mediates provioning responses to heat and land cover drives condtion, then adding land cover to the condition model might open a backdoor path and obscure the causal relationship between condition and provisioning.

Another question out of this is, are the adults responding to their own physiological state or are they responding to nestlings' condition? The tough part is that I could imagine that they're responding to nestlings' begging behavior. Does begging behavior peak at some intermediate condition (i.e. when nestlings are really hungry but not yet weakened by it), or is it strongest when nestlings are fed well?

From the reading, it looks like what we should expect is that in resource-poor environments (i.e. agriculture), provisioning should respond to quality of nestlings, whereas in resource-poor environments, provisioning should respond to need of nestlings. But also, in the short term, nestling begging rate is driven by hunger, and generally reduced in small nestlings in large broods.

## Q2H1

2. What mediates how responsive provisioning rates are to temperature?

a. (H1) Less optimal foraging conditions over the prior day will make provisioning rates less responsive to temperature because adults will respond to their chicks being hungrier when they were fed less over the prior day.

provis ~ priordaytempgoodness * tnow^2

How to measure prior day temp goodness? 
1. degree hours of difference from 35C (both cold and hot contribute to less optimal)
2. Degree hours of difference from 30C (both cold and hot contribute to less optimal)
3 Degree hours above 35C
4. Degree hours above 30C
5. Maximum temperature of the prior day


## Degree hours difference from 35C

## Q2H2

2. What mediates how responsive provisioning rates are to temperature?
 (H2) females in better condition (mass/tarsus) would be less likely than females in worse condition to reduce their visits during hot periods because they are able to mobilize the energy required to engage in more energetically costly active thermoregulatory behaviors

### How do res and condition relate to each other and to fat score?

They all look very similar to me.

```{r}

plot(res ~ condition, data = c %>% filter(Species == "WEBL"),main = "WEBL res ~ condition")
plot(res ~ `Fat Score`, data = c %>% filter(Species == "WEBL"),main = "WEBL res ~ fat")
plot(condition ~ `Fat Score`, data = c %>% filter(Species == "WEBL"), main = "WEBL condition ~ fat")

plot(res ~ condition, data = c %>% filter(Species == "TRES"),main = "TRES res ~ condition")
plot(res ~ `Fat Score`, data = c %>% filter(Species == "TRES"),main = "TRES res ~ fat")
plot(condition ~ `Fat Score`, data = c %>% filter(Species == "TRES"),main = "TRES condition ~ fat")

```

So for TRES, when females are in better body condition, there's more provisioning, and when it's hot, there's also more provisioning. But no interaction between the two.

## Q2H3

2. What mediates how responsive provisioning rates are to temperature?
c.    (H3) Females with higher baseline cort will be less responsive to temperature - possibly because they are exposing themselves to suboptimal conditions

### WEBL

```{r}
m_WEBL <- glmmTMB(valid_detections ~ poly(mean_temp_scaled,2) * cort_s1_mother_scaled + poly(tod_h_scaled,2) + mean_nestling_age_scaled + brood_size_scaled + year_fct + (1|site:attempt_id),
           family = nbinom2(),
           ziformula = ~ 1,
           data = dplyr::filter(p,!is.na(mean_temp),
                                !is.na(cort_s1_mother),
					              # !is.na(julian_date),
					              !is.na(mean_nestling_age),
					              !is.na(brood_size),
					              !is.na(tod_h),
					              !is.na(site),
					              !is.na(attempt_id),
					              !is.na(year),
					              species == "WEBL"# ,
												# tod >= hms::as.hms('11:00:00', tz = "America/Los_Angeles"),
												# tod_end <= hms::as.hms('17:00:00',tz = "America/Los_Angeles"),
												# tod_end >= hms::as.hms('11:00:00', tz = "America/Los_Angeles")
												) %>%
						mutate(across(c(tod_h,mean_temp,cort_s1_mother,julian_date,mean_nestling_age,brood_size),
													~ scale(.x)[,1],
													.names = "{.col}_scaled")), 
           )

m_WEBL_linint <- glmmTMB(valid_detections ~ mean_temp_scaled * cort_s1_mother_scaled + poly(mean_temp_scaled,degree = 2) + poly(tod_h_scaled,2) + mean_nestling_age_scaled + brood_size_scaled + year_fct + (1|site:attempt_id),
           family = nbinom2(),
           ziformula = ~ 1,
           data = dplyr::filter(p,!is.na(mean_temp),
                                !is.na(cort_s1_mother),
					              # !is.na(julian_date),
					              !is.na(mean_nestling_age),
					              !is.na(brood_size),
					              !is.na(tod_h),
					              !is.na(site),
					              !is.na(attempt_id),
					              !is.na(year),
					              species == "WEBL"# ,
												# tod >= hms::as.hms('11:00:00', tz = "America/Los_Angeles"),
												# tod_end <= hms::as.hms('17:00:00',tz = "America/Los_Angeles"),
												# tod_end >= hms::as.hms('11:00:00', tz = "America/Los_Angeles")
												) %>%
						mutate(across(c(tod_h,mean_temp,cort_s1_mother,julian_date,mean_nestling_age,brood_size),
													~ scale(.x)[,1],
													.names = "{.col}_scaled")), 
           )

m_WEBL_noint <- glmmTMB(valid_detections ~ cort_s1_mother_scaled + poly(mean_temp_scaled,degree = 2) + poly(tod_h_scaled,2) + mean_nestling_age_scaled + brood_size_scaled + year_fct + (1|site:attempt_id),
           family = nbinom2(),
           ziformula = ~ 1,
           data = dplyr::filter(p,!is.na(mean_temp),
                                !is.na(cort_s1_mother),
					              # !is.na(julian_date),
					              !is.na(mean_nestling_age),
					              !is.na(brood_size),
					              !is.na(tod_h),
					              !is.na(site),

												# tod_end <= hms::as.hms('17:00:00',tz = "America/Los_Angeles"),
												# tod_end >= hms::as.hms('11:00:00', tz = "America/Los_Angeles")
												) %>%
						mutate(across(c(tod_h,mean_temp,cort_s1_mother,julian_date,mean_nestling_age,brood_size),

(int_tab_webl_q2h3 <- comp %>%

  dplyr::select(Model,AIC,Chisq,P) %>%
  mutate(across(c(AIC,Chisq), ~ round(.x, digits = 2)),
```

## Q2H4

2. What mediates how responsive provisioning rates are to temperature?
D. (H4) Females with higher stress-induced cort will be more responsive to temperature because they have been experiencing their environment as stressful, and therefore may not have extra energy to put towards thermoregulation during hot periods.

Provis seems indifferent to cort s2 for TRES, though provis does peak at intermediate temps.

## Cort many measures


Now on to the modeling. I'm going to keep replicating the model structure from q1. Now instead of provisioning being the response, condition & cort are the response.

## Q3H1

3.   How does heat affect female body condition and stress status? baseline and stress-induced?
a.    H1: Females that experienced worse heat over the prior week will be more likely to show reduced body condition.

## Q3H2&3

b. H2: females that experienced heat over the prior day will be more likely to show elevated baseline corticosterone levels because they may upregulate their HPA axis in response to more challenging heat condition.
c.    H3: females that experienced heat over the prior week will be more likely to show elevated stress-induced corticosterone levels because challenging environmental conditions are correlated with elevated stress-induced corticosterone levels.

```{r}
  rename(`Prior day maximum temperature` = "maxt_prior_scaled",`Predicted stress-induced corticosterone` = "response",`2.5%` = "lower.CL",`97.5%` = "upper.CL" ) %>%
  group_by(`Prior day maximum temperature`) %>%
```

```{r}
data_tres_q3h3 %>% pull(attempt_id) %>% unique() %>% length()


mean_temp_tres_q3h3 <- mean(data_tres_q3h3 %>% pull(maxt_week))
sd_temp_tres_q3h3 <- sd(data_tres_q3h3 %>% pull(maxt_week))

(t <- emmeans(m_tres_q3h3,specs = "maxt_week_scaled",at = list(maxt_week_scaled = c(-1,0,2)),type = "response") %>% as.tibble() %>% #gt() %>%
  mutate(maxt_week_scaled = (maxt_week_scaled * sd_temp_tres_q3h3) + mean_temp_tres_q3h3,
    across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, digits = 2)),
    maxt_week_scaled = round(maxt_week_scaled),
    maxt_week_scaled = paste0(maxt_week_scaled,"\u00b0C")) %>%
  #tibble() %>%
  dplyr::select(-df) %>%
  #mutate(Model = rep(c("TA2 * LU + TA * LU", "TA2 + TA * LU", "TA2 + TA + LU"),2), type = c(rep("Maximum TA", 3),rep("Minimum TA",3)), .before = AIC) %>%
  rename(`Prior day maximum temperature` = "maxt_week_scaled",`Predicted stress-induced corticosterone` = "response",`2.5%` = "lower.CL",`97.5%` = "upper.CL" ) %>%
  group_by(`Prior day maximum temperature`) %>%
  mutate(row=row_number()) %>%
  pivot_longer(-c(`Prior day maximum temperature`, row)) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from=c(`Prior day maximum temperature`, name), values_from=value) %>%
  dplyr::select(-row) %>%
  #mutate(`Maximum TA_P` = if_else(`Maximum TA_P` == 0.000,"<0.001",as.character(`Maximum TA_P`))) %>%
  #mutate(`Minimum TA_P` = if_else(`Minimum TA_P` == 0.000,"<0.001",as.character(`Minimum TA_P`))) %>%
  gt() %>% tab_options(data_row.padding = px(1)) %>%
  tab_spanner_delim(
    delim="_"
  ))

gtsave(t,"../figures/tresprovisdelta_q3h3_prior.html")

((emmeans(m_tres_q3h3,specs = ~ maxt_week_scaled, at = list(maxt_week_scaled = c(2)),type = "response") %>% as.tibble() %>% pull(response))-(emmeans(m_tres_q3h3,specs = ~ maxt_week_scaled, at = list(maxt_week_scaled = c(-1)),type = "response") %>% as.tibble() %>% pull(response)))/(emmeans(m_tres_q3h3,specs = ~ maxt_week_scaled, at = list(maxt_week_scaled = c(-1)),type = "response") %>% as.tibble() %>% pull(response))



temp_trans_tres_q3h3 <- trans_new("temp_trans_tres_q3h3",
                             transform = function(x){(x * sd_temp_tres_q3h3) + mean_temp_tres_q3h3},
                             inverse = function(x){x})

(figq3h3_tres <- predict_response(m_tres_q3h3,terms = c("maxt_week_scaled [-2.5:2.5 by=.1]"),margin = "empirical") %>%
    plot(line_size = 1.5,alpha = .2,show_data = TRUE,limit_range = TRUE) +
    aes(linetype = .data[["group"]]) +
    theme_classic() +
    # facet_wrap(~ group, ncol = 2) +
    xlab("Prior week average daily maximum temperature (\u00b0C)") +
    ylab("Stress-induced corticosterone (ng/uL)") +
    scale_fill_viridis(discrete = TRUE) +
    scale_color_viridis(discrete = TRUE) +
    theme(text = element_text(size = 16)) +
    labs(title =  "TRES stress-induced cort: max * LC interaction") +
    scale_x_continuous(trans = temp_trans_tres_q3h3,
                       breaks = c((20-mean_temp_tres_q3h3)/sd_temp_tres_q3h3,
                                  (25-mean_temp_tres_q3h3)/sd_temp_tres_q3h3,
                                  (30-mean_temp_tres_q3h3)/sd_temp_tres_q3h3,
                                  (35-mean_temp_tres_q3h3)/sd_temp_tres_q3h3,
                                  (40-mean_temp_tres_q3h3)/sd_temp_tres_q3h3),
                       # breaks = c(20,30,40,50),
                       # labels = c("20","30","40","50"),
                       # limits = c((15-mean(g$meanmaxtempI,na.rm = TRUE))/sd(g$meanmaxtempI,na.rm = TRUE),
                       #            (55-mean(g$meanmaxtempI,na.rm = TRUE))/sd(g$meanmaxtempI,na.rm = TRUE))
                       # limits = c(18,5)
    ) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = "solid") +
    #ylim(-5,5) +
    geom_text(data = dat_text_tres_q3h3, mapping = aes(x = -Inf, y = Inf,label = label),hjust = -.2, vjust = 4,inherit.aes = FALSE) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
)

ggsave("../figures/provisbymaxtempxhab_TRES_q3h3.png",plot =  figq3h3_tres, width = 10, height = 6.6)
```
